questions.q: Why does Project 1 write out definitions (pipeline, win rate, coverage, and so on) before building any report?
options: Because Salesforce refuses to run reports without a written definition
Because many analytics disagreements are really disagreements about what a metric means
Because definitions are only needed for dashboards, not reports
Because definitions make the data load faster
questions.explain: Agreeing on definitions first prevents two people from getting different numbers for the same-named metric.

questions.q: In this project, what is the quarterly quota per rep at Alder & Vale Systems?
questions.explain: $9.0M per year across six reps is $1.5M each per year, or $375K per rep per quarter.

questions.q: How is coverage defined in this project?
options: Closed Won this quarter divided by quarterly quota
Open pipeline closing this quarter divided by the remaining gap to quota
Won deals divided by lost deals
Total leads divided by total accounts
questions.explain: Coverage compares open pipeline that could close this quarter to how much revenue is still needed. Attainment is the won-divided-by-quota measure.

questions.q: The project's numbers are described as illustrative. What should you take from that?
options: Your org's numbers should match them exactly
The numbers are real customer figures
Your numbers will differ; what matters is that your method is sound and you can explain each number
You should not build the reports at all
questions.explain: The baseline exists so you can sanity-check the kind of answer your reports produce, not to be reproduced digit for digit.

questions.q: Which set lists the sales reps at Alder & Vale Systems correctly?
options: Maya Ortiz, Dev Patel, Lena Fischer, Marcus Reid, Priya Nair, Tomas Silva
Only Maya Ortiz and Dev Patel
Twelve unnamed agents
Marcus Reid, Priya Nair, and the VP of Sales only
questions.explain: The sales team has six reps, and their names stay the same across every lesson in the course.
